en: So complex or deep that few people can grasp it
hook: ABSTRUSE: ABSTRACT and CONFUSE.
story: Abstruse. So complex or deep that few people can grasp it. In her first week at a philosophy reading circle, Leah opened a translated page of Kant. She read one sentence five times and still could not say what it meant. The room was silent except for the ceiling fan. [sigh] Even the circle's leader admitted the text was abstruse. Abstruse comes from a Latin word meaning thrust away and hidden, as if the meaning had been pushed out of reach. So, what word describes writing so deep that few people can follow it? ... Abstruse.

gre.s: Although the philosopher's early essays were lucid and accessible, his later work grew so ____ that even specialists confessed they could not follow its arguments.
gre.clue: even specialists confessed they could not follow its arguments

example: Rahim gave up on the abstruse tax manual and simply asked an accountant in Motijheel to fill in his return.

en: Excessively eager to acquire money or possessions
hook: ACQUISITIVE: always ACQUIRING more.
story: Acquisitive. Too eager to gain money or possessions. Every Friday, Neil's uncle drives out to a new housing project on the edge of the city. He already owns three flats and a shop, yet he keeps a folder of land deals beside his bed and talks about plots at every family dinner. When Neil asked what he would do with one more flat, his uncle had no answer. Acquisitive shares its root with acquire: an acquisitive person can never stop acquiring. So, what word describes someone hungry to keep gaining more and more possessions? ... Acquisitive.

gre.s: Far from being content with his considerable wealth, the tycoon remained relentlessly ____, buying up rival companies merely to add them to his holdings.
gre.clue: buying up rival companies merely to add them to his holdings

example: In an acquisitive age, the monk's tiny room with one blanket and a few books struck visitors as a quiet rebuke.

en: To persuade someone through flattery or gentle, persistent coaxing
bn: তোষামোদ করে রাজি করানো; ভুলিয়ে-ভালিয়ে রাজি করানো
hook: CAJOLE: CAGE them with sweet words, JOLLY them along.
story: Cajole. To persuade someone with flattery or gentle, patient coaxing. Molly wanted to join her class trip to the beach, but her father said no. So every evening she made his favourite ginger tea, praised his old cricket stories, and asked again, softly. On the fifth night he put down his cup, [chuckle] and said, "All right, go." Molly [laugh] threw her arms around him. She had cajoled him into it. Hear the word jolly hiding inside cajole: you jolly someone along until they give in. So, what verb means to coax someone with sweet words until they agree? ... Cajole.

gre.s: Unable to force the stubborn witness to testify, the detective tried instead to ____ him, offering compliments and small favors until he agreed to talk.
gre.clue: offering compliments and small favors

example: Sadia cajoled her little brother into finishing his homework by promising him an extra hour of football.

en: Rude and bad-tempered in a mean-spirited way
hook: CHURLISH: a grumpy CHURL who growls at everyone.
story: Churlish. Rude and bad-tempered in a mean-spirited way. On a cold January morning, Jody carried a plate of warm steamed rice cakes up to the new neighbour. He opened the door, frowned at the plate, and said, "I did not ask for this." Then he shut the door. Jody stood on the stairs, her cheeks burning. It was a churlish answer to a kind gift. A churl was a rough peasant in old English, and churlish first meant behaving like one, without any courtesy. So, what word describes a rude, ungracious response to kindness? ... Churlish.

gre.s: It would be ____ to criticize the volunteers' modest fundraiser, given how generously they had donated their own time.
gre.clue: given how generously they had donated their own time

example: The guest's churlish refusal to thank his hosts for the elaborate wedding feast embarrassed his entire family.

en: Sad and disappointed
hook: CREST-FALLEN: a rooster whose proud crest has drooped.
story: Crestfallen. Sad and disappointed after a hope collapses. Shane's school team needed one run off the last ball of the district final. He swung hard, missed, and heard the stumps rattle behind him. He walked off with his head down and his bat dragging in the dust, too crestfallen to look at his friends. His coach walked over and put an arm around the crestfallen boy. Picture a proud rooster whose red crest has drooped and fallen: that is what crestfallen looks like. So, what word describes someone deflated by a sudden disappointment? ... Crestfallen.

gre.s: The usually confident candidate looked ____ as the results came in, his campaign having fallen far short of expectations.
gre.clue: having fallen far short of expectations

example: Imran looked crestfallen when the publisher returned his first manuscript with a polite but firm rejection letter.

en: Cheerful and full of energy; bubbling with enthusiasm
hook: EBULLIENT: BUBBLING over like boiling water.
story: Ebullient. Cheerful and bubbling with energy. When Ivy's younger brother got into the engineering university, he burst through the front door shouting the news. He hugged their mother, [laugh] danced with their grandmother, called every cousin, and ran down to the corner shop to buy sweets for the whole lane. Even at midnight he was still ebullient, talking too fast to finish a sentence. Ebullient comes from the Latin for boiling over, and an ebullient person bubbles over with joy, like milk rising in a pot. So, what word describes someone overflowing with cheerful energy? ... Ebullient.

gre.s: Normally reserved and soft-spoken, the professor was uncharacteristically ____ at the reception, laughing loudly and greeting every guest with a warm embrace.
gre.clue: laughing loudly and greeting every guest with a warm embrace

example: The ebullient fans poured into the streets of Chattogram, dancing and waving flags after the late winning goal.

en: Worthy of great respect
hook: ESTIMABLE: held in high ESTEEM.
story: Estimable. Worthy of great respect. For thirty-five years, Headmaster Albert Kerr cycled to a village school, through mud in the monsoon and fog in winter. He taught poor students for free in the evenings and never missed a day. When he retired, former students came from the city and even from abroad to touch his feet. He was an estimable man, and his estimable life filled the school field with gratitude. Estimable comes from the same root as esteem: an estimable person is held in high esteem. So, what word describes someone deeply worthy of respect? ... Estimable.

gre.s: Despite their political differences, even the senator's rivals regarded him as thoroughly ____, a public servant whose integrity had never once been questioned.
gre.clue: whose integrity had never once been questioned

example: The retiring headmistress was an estimable woman who had taught three generations of the same village families.

en: Quickly fading or disappearing
hook: EVANESCENT: EVAPORATES and VANISHES.
story: Evanescent. Quickly fading or disappearing. Every autumn morning, Amber's grandmother gathered night jasmine flowers from the wet grass under the tree, white petals with bright orange stems, fallen in the night. By the time the sun was high, they had wilted, and their sweet smell was gone. "Pick them early," she would say. "Their beauty is evanescent." Evanescent shares its root with vanish: something evanescent vanishes almost as soon as it appears. So, what word describes beauty that fades away almost at once? ... Evanescent.

gre.s: The perfume's scent proved ____, fading within minutes of being applied despite the manufacturer's promise that it would last all day.
gre.clue: fading within minutes

example: Social media fame is often evanescent, and last month's viral singer may already be forgotten by her followers.

en: Needing to be dealt with right away
hook: EXIGENT: an EMERGENT, EXTREME need.
story: Exigent. Pressing; needing attention right away. The night before the board exams, the river swept away the road from Kyle's river island village. Three hundred students had to reach the exam centre by nine in the morning. The headmaster rang the boat owners one by one, and by dawn a line of engine boats waited at the bank. It was an exigent situation, and exigent needs leave no room for delay. Exigent shares its root with exact, from a Latin verb meaning to demand. So, what word describes a situation that demands action right now? ... Exigent.

gre.s: Because the circumstances were so ____, with the floodwaters rising by the hour, officials bypassed the usual approval process and evacuated the town at once.
gre.clue: with the floodwaters rising by the hour

example: Facing exigent demands from creditors, the small garment factory sold two of its machines to cover the wages.

en: Interchangeable; replaceable by another identical item
hook: FUNGIBLE: FUN to swap, since one is as good as another.
story: Fungible. Interchangeable; one unit can be replaced by another identical one. When Ron borrowed a kilo of sugar from his neighbour, he returned a different kilo the next day, and nobody minded. Sugar is fungible. But when he borrowed her fountain pen, a gift from her grandfather, and lost it, no new pen could take its place. Ron felt sick with shame. Fungible comes from a Latin verb meaning to perform: one fungible item can perform the job of another. So, what word describes things that can be swapped one for another, like dollar bills? ... Fungible.

gre.s: Unlike works of art, which are unique, commodities such as wheat are ____: one bushel can be substituted for another without any loss of value.
gre.clue: one bushel can be substituted for another without any loss of value

example: Banknotes are fungible, so it makes no difference which particular thousand-taka note the cashier hands you.

en: Harmful or hostile; tending to obstruct
hook: INIMICAL: contains 'enemy' (inimicus in Latin).
story: Inimical. Harmful or hostile; working against something. On the low southern coast, farmers like Roy's father once grew rice on every field. Then salt water from the sea crept further inland each year, and the soil turned white and crusty at the edges. Salt is inimical to rice; the young plants turn yellow and die. Now many families farm shrimp instead. Inimical comes from the Latin inimicus, an enemy, the opposite of amicus, a friend: an inimical force acts like an enemy. So, what word describes conditions that are harmful or hostile to something? ... Inimical.

gre.s: Constant noise and interruptions are ____ to the deep concentration that serious writing demands.
gre.clue: the deep concentration that serious writing demands

example: Soaring rents in the city center have proved inimical to the small bookshops that once lined the old streets.

en: Untruthfulness; the habit of lying
hook: MENDACITY: MEN DARE lie.
story: Mendacity. Untruthfulness; the habit of lying. A land broker sold Tyler's father a plot he swore was free of any dispute. Later they learned that three other families had bought the very same plot. When Tyler confronted him, the broker invented a new story every week: a lost file, a sick clerk, a mistake at the land office. His mendacity seemed to have no end. Mendacity comes from the Latin mendax, meaning lying; do not confuse it with mendicant, which means a beggar. So, what noun means a habit of telling lies? ... Mendacity.

gre.s: The memoir was celebrated as a model of candor until journalists exposed its author's ____: many of its most moving episodes had simply been invented.
gre.clue: many of its most moving episodes had simply been invented

example: Once the auditors revealed the chairman's mendacity, shareholders demanded to know how many earlier reports had been invented.

en: Someone who commits crimes or misbehaves
hook: MIS-CREANT: a MIS-CREATED person who does wrong.
story: Miscreant. Someone who behaves badly or breaks the law. Every Friday, worshippers at a city mosque came out after prayers to find that someone had stolen their best sandals. One week, a young volunteer named Zack watched the shoe racks. He caught the miscreant, a grown man with a plastic bag full of sandals. The imam shook his head as the police led the miscreant away. The old French word meant unbelieving, so a miscreant was first a heretic, then any wrongdoer. So, what noun means a person who does wrong or breaks the law? ... Miscreant.

gre.s: The townspeople regarded the young man as a hopeless ____ until he returned the stolen money and spent years volunteering to repay his debt to the community.
gre.clue: returned the stolen money

example: Security cameras finally caught the miscreants who had been slashing bicycle tires outside the university hostel.

en: Fashionable; stylish
hook: MODISH: MODERN and in MODE (fashion).
story: Modish. Fashionable and stylish, in tune with the latest trend. Natalie walked into the holiday gathering in a handwoven sari with silver sneakers, a look she had first seen online only a week before. Her cousins [gasp] crowded around to take pictures. Everyone agreed it was the most modish outfit in the room. By next year, of course, the same look would feel old. Think of the word mode, which in French means fashion: whatever is modish is in the current mode. So, what word describes something fashionable right now? ... Modish.

gre.s: The restaurant's décor, so ____ when it opened a decade ago, now looks hopelessly dated, a relic of a style no one wants anymore.
gre.clue: now looks hopelessly dated

example: In the 1960s, modish young women in Dhaka wore bouffant hairstyles copied from the posters of popular film stars.

en: Too eager to please or obey; excessively flattering
hook: OBSEQUIOUS: 'obsessively SEEK to please us'.
story: Obsequious. Too eager to please or obey; flattering in an embarrassing way. At Mitch's office downtown, one clerk jumped up every time the director walked in. He praised the director's ties, laughed loudest at his jokes, and once ran down three floors to fetch an umbrella nobody had asked for. His coworkers [sigh] traded tired looks at each obsequious display. Obsequious holds the Latin root sequi, to follow, as in sequence: an obsequious person follows the boss everywhere, bowing. So, what word describes someone who flatters and obeys far too eagerly? ... Obsequious.

gre.s: The courtiers' ____ praise of the king, which never wavered even when his decrees were absurd, revealed more fear than admiration.
gre.clue: never wavered even when his decrees were absurd

example: The new manager grew tired of the obsequious clerk who agreed with every remark and laughed at every joke.

en: Serving as a typical or perfect example of something
hook: PARADIGM = a model. PARADIGMATIC = the model example.
story: Paradigmatic. Serving as a typical or perfect example of something. When Professor Nash teaches essay writing, she always hands out one old answer by a former student named Rosa. It opens with a clear claim, gives three strong examples, and ends with a quiet, confident conclusion. Year after year, students study it line by line. It has become the paradigmatic essay, the model for all the rest. A paradigm is a model or pattern, so something paradigmatic is the model example of its kind. So, what word describes a perfect, textbook example of something? ... Paradigmatic.

gre.s: The trial has become ____, cited in nearly every textbook as the classic example of judicial overreach.
gre.clue: the classic example

example: For many economists, the rise of the garment industry is the paradigmatic case of export-led growth in a poor country.

en: Very reluctant to spend money; tight with cash
hook: PARSIMONIOUS: PARSING every penny, unwilling to spend.
story: Parsimonious. Extremely unwilling to spend money. Ian's landlord owns two city buildings, yet he refuses to fix the broken staircase light. Tenants climb the dark stairs by the glow of their phones. When the water pump failed in June, he waited a whole week, hoping it would mend itself, rather than pay a mechanic. Even his own children call him parsimonious. Parsimonious comes from the Latin for sparing: a parsimonious person spares every coin, even when spending is badly needed. So, what word describes someone painfully tight with money? ... Parsimonious.

gre.s: The billionaire was so ____ that he installed pay phones in his mansion so that guests would have to pay for their own calls.
gre.clue: installed pay phones in his mansion

example: The parsimonious landlord refused to replace a single broken bulb in the stairwell, so tenants climbed in darkness.

en: A remark used too often to be interesting or meaningful
hook: PLATITUDE: a FLAT attitude remark; flat, dull, overused.
story: Platitude. A remark used so often that it has lost its meaning. When Frank missed the medical admission cut-off by a few marks, relatives called one after another. "Everything happens for a reason." "Failure is the pillar of success." Each platitude landed like a pat on the head, kind but empty. Only his sister said something real: "Let us go through your weak chapters together tomorrow." Platitude comes from the French plat, meaning flat: a platitude is a flat, worn-out saying. So, what noun means a tired, overused remark? ... Platitude.

gre.s: The commencement speaker disappointed the graduates by offering nothing but ____, urging them to follow their dreams and never give up.
gre.clue: urging them to follow their dreams and never give up

example: When the coach offered only the platitude that winning is not everything, the defeated players rolled their eyes.

en: Easily bent; easily influenced
hook: PLIANT: PLIABLE, bends easily.
story: Pliant. Easily bent; also, easily influenced by others. In a craft village, Tara watched a weaver soak cane strips in water until they turned soft. Then the strips curved in his hands without a single crack, becoming the round wall of a basket. "Dry cane snaps," he said. "Wet cane is pliant." People can be pliant too, bending to whoever speaks loudest. Pliant shares its root with pliable, from a French verb meaning to bend or fold. So, what word describes something that bends easily, or a person easily swayed? ... Pliant.

gre.s: The dictator surrounded himself with ____ advisers who never challenged his decisions, however reckless.
gre.clue: who never challenged his decisions

example: Weavers soak the cane strips overnight until they become pliant enough to be bent into baskets without cracking.

en: A person with expert knowledge in many subjects
hook: POLY = many, MATH = learning. Learned in many things.
story: Polymath. A person with expert knowledge in many different subjects. In a school library, Piper found an old book about a great scientist from Bengal. He studied radio waves, built delicate instruments to measure how plants respond to the world, and even wrote one of the earliest science fiction stories in his mother tongue. Piper [gasp] read until the librarian rang the closing bell. She had found a true polymath. Poly means many, and math comes from a Greek word for learning, so a polymath has learned many things. So, what do you call a person brilliant in many fields? ... Polymath.

gre.s: A true ____, she published influential papers in physics, composed music, and wrote two acclaimed novels.
gre.clue: published influential papers in physics, composed music, and wrote two acclaimed novels

example: Rabindranath Tagore was a polymath who wrote novels, composed thousands of songs, painted, and founded a university.

en: To be a sign or warning that something, usually bad, is likely to happen
hook: PORTEND: POR-TEND, a portent, an omen of what's coming.
story: Portend. To be a sign that something, usually bad, is coming. In late June, Rita's family watched the great river climb a little higher every evening. The water swallowed the first step of the landing, then the second. Heavy rain had been falling upstream for a week. To the old farmers, these signs portended a flood, and they began moving rice and goats to higher ground. Portend comes from the Latin for stretching forward, like a sign that points ahead to what is coming. So, what verb means to be a warning sign of future trouble? ... Portend.

gre.s: Economists worry that the sudden drop in consumer spending may ____ a deeper recession in the coming year.
gre.clue: a deeper recession in the coming year

example: Several resignations from the board in one week portended trouble for the struggling airline.

en: To hint that something, often bad, is coming; such a hint
hook: PRE-SAGE: a SAGE who tells the future BEFORE it happens.
story: Presage. To be a sign of something coming, often something bad; as a noun, the sign itself. On Monday, the teacher at Zane's coaching centre handed out an easy quant sheet with an unusual smile. "Enjoy this one," he said. The students groaned, because they knew that smile. It always presaged a brutal mock test on Friday. Zane [chuckle] shook his head; that smile had never been a false presage. Pre means before, so picture a wise sage who sees trouble before it arrives. So, what word means to hint that something, often bad, is on its way? ... Presage.

gre.s: Some economists warned that the sudden drop in consumer spending could ____ a deeper recession, while others insisted it was merely a seasonal fluctuation.
gre.clue: while others insisted it was merely a seasonal fluctuation

example: The first cuckoo calls in the mango groves presage the arrival of spring in rural Bengal.

en: Showing unhealthy curiosity about sex or scandal
hook: PRURIENT: like an ITCH (prurire = to itch) for scandal.
story: Prurient. Showing an unhealthy interest in sex or scandal. When a young couple in Rita's apartment building quietly divorced, some neighbours could talk of nothing else. They gathered on the stairs, guessing at bedroom secrets, and one aunt even tried to read the couple's mail. Rita felt uneasy and walked away. Their prurient curiosity had nothing to do with care. Prurient comes from a Latin verb meaning to itch: a prurient mind itches for private details that are none of its business. So, what word describes an unhealthy curiosity about other people's intimate lives and scandals? ... Prurient.

gre.s: Critics charged that the documentary, despite its claims to serious journalism, merely catered to viewers' ____ curiosity, lingering on lurid details of the celebrity's private affairs.
gre.clue: lingering on lurid details of the celebrity's private affairs

example: The tabloid's prurient coverage of the actress's divorce sold many copies but told readers nothing worth knowing.

en: Always ready to pick a fight or argue
hook: PUGNACIOUS: ready to throw a PUNCH, like a pug that barks at everyone.
story: Pugnacious. Eager to argue or fight. Every morning on the bus into town, Sally saw the same passenger pick a quarrel. One day it was the conductor's change, the next a stranger's elbow, then the driver's music. His voice rose, his finger jabbed the air, and the whole bus went tense whenever he climbed aboard. He was the most pugnacious man on the route. Pugnacious comes from the Latin for fighting with the fist, like pugilist, an old word for a boxer. So, what word describes someone always spoiling for a fight? ... Pugnacious.

gre.s: The usually ____ senator surprised observers by conceding the point calmly instead of launching into one of his customary attacks.
gre.clue: instead of launching into one of his customary attacks

example: The pugnacious little terrier barked at every delivery van on the street, no matter how large.

en: Formidable, especially as an opponent; worthy of respect
hook: RE-DOUBT-ABLE: you DOUBT you can beat them.
story: Redoubtable. Formidable, especially as an opponent; worthy of fearful respect. In Sean's lane in the old city, nobody wanted to face his grandmother at the carrom board. At seventy, she flicked the striker with one finger and sank the queen as if it were nothing. Young men who boasted at the start went home silent. [laugh] She was a redoubtable opponent. Redoubtable comes from an old French verb meaning to dread: a redoubtable rival is someone you dread to face. So, what word describes an opponent so formidable that others fear to challenge her? ... Redoubtable.

gre.s: Even seasoned lawyers dreaded facing her in court, for she was a ____ advocate whose cross-examinations had demolished countless witnesses.
gre.clue: whose cross-examinations had demolished countless witnesses

example: The visiting team knew they faced a redoubtable bowling attack on the spin-friendly pitch at Mirpur.

en: To turn something over in your mind for a long time
hook: RUMINATE: like a cow chewing cud, chewing a thought over and over.
story: Ruminate. To think about something deeply, for a long time. In a quiet village, Nora watched the family cow lying under the jackfruit tree, slowly chewing the same mouthful of grass. Nora was doing much the same with a letter from a university in Japan. All afternoon she ruminated: leave her ageing parents, or stay? Ruminate comes from the Latin for chewing the cud, so to ruminate is to chew on an idea. So, what verb means to turn a thought over and over in your mind? ... Ruminate.

gre.s: Instead of acting decisively, the general would ____ for days over every decision, by which time the opportunity had usually passed.
gre.clue: Instead of acting decisively

example: Sitting on the rooftop after midnight, Arif ruminated on whether to accept the scholarship that would take him abroad.

en: Clever but deliberately misleading argument
hook: SOPHISTRY: from the SOPHISTS, Greek teachers who could argue anything.
story: Sophistry. A clever argument that is deliberately misleading. Andy's younger brother wanted to skip his maths homework. "If the teacher never checks homework, then homework does not really exist," he announced at dinner, "and nobody can do what does not exist." For a moment the table went quiet. Then their father [laugh] said, "Very clever. Now go and do it." It was pure sophistry. The word comes from the Sophists, ancient Greek teachers famous for arguing any side for a fee. So, what noun means a clever argument designed to mislead? ... Sophistry.

gre.s: The lawyer's defense, though dazzlingly clever, was mere ____: each step seemed logical, yet the argument as a whole was designed to mislead the jury.
gre.clue: designed to mislead the jury

example: The debate judges saw through the team's sophistry, noting that its clever statistics proved nothing about the actual motion.

en: Cloudy or muddy (of liquid); confused
hook: TURBID: TURBulent water, all stirred up.
story: Turbid. Cloudy and muddy, as a liquid is when stirred up; also, confused. In August, Shelby took the ferry across the great river. The river that had looked green in winter was now thick and brown, swirling with silt, sticks and clumps of water hyacinth. When he dipped his hand in, he could not see his own fingers. The water was turbid from bank to bank. Turbid shares its root with disturb and turbulent: turbid water has been disturbed until it clouds. So, what word describes water so muddy and stirred up that you cannot see through it? ... Turbid.

gre.s: Once so clear that visitors could see pebbles three meters down, the lake has become ____ since mining began upstream, its waters now thick with silt.
gre.clue: its waters now thick with silt

example: After the monsoon rains, the Padma runs turbid and brown, carrying tons of sediment toward the Bay of Bengal.

en: Serving as a farewell
hook: VALEDICTORY: say VALE (farewell).
story: Valedictory. Serving as a farewell. After thirty years delivering letters in a quiet village, the postman Harold gave a short valedictory speech under the banyan tree. He remembered the wedding cards he had carried and the letters from sons working abroad that he had placed in their mothers' hands. Old women wiped their eyes with the ends of their saris. It was the warmest valedictory moment the village had seen. Vale is Latin for farewell, and dicere means to say: valedictory words say goodbye. So, what word describes a speech given as a farewell? ... Valedictory.

gre.s: The retiring minister's ____ speech, delivered on her final day in parliament, graciously thanked even her fiercest opponents for decades of spirited debate.
gre.clue: delivered on her final day in parliament

example: In his valedictory column after forty years at the newspaper, the editor thanked the readers who had argued with him most.

en: The appearance of being true or real
hook: VERI-SIMILI-TUDE: VERY SIMILAR to truth.
story: Verisimilitude. The quality of seeming true or real. Before writing her novel about tea garden workers in the hills, Sharon spent two months living near the estate. She learned how the pluckers pick two leaves and a bud, the songs they hum on the slopes, and the smell of the factory at dawn. When readers finished the book, many asked whether it was a true story. That was its verisimilitude. Veri means true, as in verify, and simil means like, as in similar: verisimilitude is being like the truth. So, what noun means the appearance of being real? ... Verisimilitude.

gre.s: The novel's historical details lend it a striking ____, though every one of its characters is invented.
gre.clue: though every one of its characters is invented

example: To add verisimilitude to the war film, the director cast actual veterans and filmed in the villages where battles had occurred.
